title: Piel
description: Learn the Piel stem and its intensive and factitive meanings.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Piel is the intensive stem. Its mark is the doubling of the middle root letter, both in verbs and in the nouns that come from them. The perfect has i in the first syllable and usually e in the second (קִטֵּל), and the stem inflects exactly like Qal. In meaning Piel adds intensity or iteration — "he broke in pieces" against "he broke" — and it often carries a causative or factitive force.

blocks.caption: The doubling
blocks.html: The doubled middle radical is the signature of the intensive. Piel's perfect is קִטֵּל (i in the first syllable, e in the second); its imperfect is יְקַטֵּל. When the middle radical is a guttural, which cannot be doubled, the preceding vowel lengthens instead — a change you will meet again in the guttural chapters.

blocks.caption: The meanings
blocks.html: Piel properly intensifies the Qal: שָׁבַר, "he broke", but שִׁבֵּר, "he broke in pieces"; שָׁאַל, "he asked", but שִׁאֵל, "he begged". Because eagerness often urges others to the same action, Piel sometimes has a causative force: לָמַד, "he learned", but לִמֵּד, "he taught". Let the context choose among these shades.

blocks.caption: Nouns from the intensive
blocks.html: The doubled middle letter also forms nouns, and these frequently name a person who practices a trade or profession — one who performs the act habitually. Thus גַּנָּב, "a thief", and טַבָּח, "a cook". Seeing the doubled letter in a noun is a clue that it belongs to this intensive family.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not force "intensive" onto every Piel. It is a tendency, not a rule, and the dictionary decides the exact sense. Also keep the vowel of the perfect in mind: i in the first syllable and usually e in the second, because this is what distinguishes Piel from Qal at a glance.

blocks.caption: Worked example
blocks.html: Take דִּבֵּר ("he spoke"). The doubled bet and the i–e vowels mark Piel against Qal דָּבַר ("he said"). The doubling is the sign of the intensive, and the same root in Piel shifts its meaning toward deliberate, sustained speaking. When you see a doubled middle letter with i–e, parse Piel.

blocks.caption: Reading practice
blocks.html: Read and parse. דִּבֵּר הָאִישׁ — "the man spoke" (Piel). בֵּרֵךְ אֶת־הָעָם — "he blessed the people". The doubled middle letter with the i–e vowels marks Piel; translate with the intensive or factitive force the context calls for.
